Below is a taxonomy of commonly-used techniques for manipulating visible and invisible watermarks in images—focusing strictly on creative, legal, “art-for-art’s-sake” applications.  (Techniques intended to *remove* someone else’s watermark without permission are both unethical and may breach copyright law; those are omitted here.)

1. Visible-Watermark Stylization  
   • Opacity & Blend Modes  
     – Adjust watermark opacity (10–70%) so it reads as a ghosted layer  
     – Experiment with Photoshop/GIMP blend modes (Multiply, Screen, Overlay, Soft Light) to integrate the watermark into highlights, midtones or shadows  
   • Color & Tone Mapping  
     – Map watermark to a complementary or monochrome palette (e.g. desaturate + tint)  
     – Use gradient maps to turn flat logos into duotone or tritone elements  
   • Warping & Distortion  
     – Apply Photoshop’s Warp, Liquify or Puppet Warp to bend the watermark around image features  
     – Use displacement maps (generated from the photo’s luminance) so the watermark subtly follows underlying texture  
   • Texture & Embossing  
     – Overlay the watermark as a bump or displacement map on a 3D surface  
     – Apply Bevel & Emboss, Grain or Noise filters so the watermark mimics paper grain, halftone dots or paint cracks  
   • Glitch & “Datamosh” Effects  
     – Export the PNG/JPEG as raw video frames, then use simple datamosh tools (e.g. FFmpeg frame dropping) to create compression artifacts that glitch the watermark  
     – Instillations: animate the watermark’s pixel-sorting or channel-shifts as an audiovisual effect  

2. Vector-Based & Generative Watermarks  
   • SVG Deformation  
     – Load logo/vector watermark into Illustrator or Inkscape, then apply path-simplify, twist, or envelope deformations  
     – Export multiple intermediate t-frames and blend in a time-lapse or animation  
   • Parametric & Procedural Art  
     – Feed watermark outlines as seed curves into Processing/p5.js or TouchDesigner to generate particle trails, L-systems or flow fields  
     – Animate these generativeforms so the watermark “grows” or “decays” across the canvas  
   • Shader & GPU Effects  
     – In Unity/Unreal or GLSL/WebGL, map the watermark as a texture input to custom shaders (e.g. Voronoi distortion, sine-wave ripples)  
     – Use time or audio input to drive real-time distortion  

3. Interactive & Augmented-Reality Presentations  
   • Hover/Click Reveals  
     – In web-based projects, mask the watermark until mouseover or touch—then transition it into full opacity or color  
   • AR Filters  
     – In Spark AR or Lens Studio, anchor a watermark graphic to real-world surfaces or user faces, then let users “paint” or warp it with gestures  
   • Projection-Mapped Installations  
     – Treat the watermark as its own video layer in MadMapper or TouchDesigner; project onto 3D objects so it scales/warps physically  

4. Invisible/Digital Watermark Embedding (Artistic Variants)  
   While normally used for copyright tracking, you can repurpose them as “hidden” layers that only specialized viewers or scripts will reveal—an effect in many net-art projects.  
   • Spatial-Domain LSB (Least Significant Bit)  
     – Embed a low-opacity logo in the image’s least significant bitplane; it remains invisible to the eye but can be extracted algorithmically  
   • Frequency-Domain Transforms  
     – DCT-based (JPEG) or DWT-based (wavelet) embedding: slightly modify mid-frequency coefficients so the watermark “lives” under compression  
     – Artistic twist: publish both “clean” and “marked” versions and let viewers toggle a slider to reveal hidden messages or designs  
   • Patchwork/Spread-Spectrum  
     – Subdivide the image into a pseudo-random pattern and add tiny cloned fragments of the watermark across it—no one patch is legible alone, but an extractor reassembles them  
   • Application  
     – Create limited-edition prints that look identical until scanned with a smartphone app that reconstructs the hidden watermark  
     – Embed cryptic QR-codes or glyphs that only appear after a high-pass or edge-detect filter, evoking a “secret code” aesthetic  

5. Toolchains & Workflows  
   • Photoshop/GIMP + Illustrator/Inkscape  
     – Best for combined pixel/vector workflows, quick mask/blend adjustments, displacement maps  
   • Affinity Photo/Designer  
     – Similar to Adobe suite but lower cost—supports PSD and SVG manipulation  
   • Blender/After Effects  
     – For 3D-mapped watermarks, dynamic lighting, camera‐mapped texturing, animated dissolves  
   • Open-Source Code Libraries  
     – Python + OpenCV: script batch warps, color-space manipulations, pixel-sorting  
     – p5.js/Processing: generative patterns driven by watermark geometry  
     – FFmpeg: frame-level glitch/datamosh pipelines  

6. Practical & Legal Tips  
   • Always work on copies and maintain an unaltered master.  
   • If you’re using someone else’s logo or brand-mark artistically, secure written permission or operate under fair-use guidelines.  
   • Avoid instructing or implementing *watermark removal* on copyrighted material—it’s both unethical and possibly illegal.  

By combining these approaches—layer blending, vector deformation, procedural generation, invisible twists—you can turn a simple watermark into an integral, dynamic element of your visual artwork rather than an afterthought.

Here’s a tool-by-tool breakdown of practical techniques—mostly non-destructive—for turning a watermark into a seamless, “of-the-scene” element rather than an afterthought.  Whenever possible work on a copy or in a linked/smart-object workflow.

1. Adobe Photoshop  
   • Import as Smart Object  
     – File→Place Embedded/Linked. Keeps your watermark editable.  
   • Blend Modes & Opacity  
     – Experiment with Overlay, Soft Light, Hard Light or Screen/Multiply at 10–60% opacity.  
     – Use the “Blend If…” sliders (double-click layer → Blending Options) to make the mark only show in highlights or shadows.  
   • Color & Tone Matching  
     – Create a clipped Adjustment Layer (Hue/Saturation, Curves or Gradient Map) above the watermark. Tweak so its tonal range matches the photo.  
     – Use Color Lookup Tables (3DLUTs) clipped to the watermark for one-click grading.  
   • Displacement Mapping  
     – Generate a displacement map from your background: duplicate the base, desaturate & high-pass to enhance edges, save as PSD.  
     – Filter→Distort→Displace on watermark Smart Object, so it subtly “rides” over textures.  
   • Layer Masks & Brushes  
     – Mask out the watermark edges with a soft/bristled brush to blend into shadows or around objects.  
     – Paint low-opacity soft shadows (with a dark, low-flow brush) around the watermark to anchor it.  
   • Textures & Noise  
     – Add Filter→Noise→Add Noise (Gaussian, ~2–5%) clipped to watermark so it shares film-grain or sensor noise.  
     – Use Filter→Texture→Grain for paper- or canvas-style art.  
   • Liquify & Warp  
     – Filter→Liquify or Edit→Transform→Warp/Perspective to bend the logo around 3D shapes (e.g. folds in fabric).  
     – Puppet Warp for more control over “pin” placement.  

2. Affinity Photo (similar to Photoshop)  
   • Live Filter Layers  
     – Add a Live Liquify, Live Noise or High Pass clipped to your watermark. You can toggle/edit them later.  
   • Layer Effects  
     – Outer Glow or Inner Shadow to emulate backlit or embossed effects.  
     – Gradient Overlay to introduce duotone or tritone coloring.  
   • Adjustment Clips  
     – Drag any Adjustment Layer (HSL, Curves, LUT) into the watermark layer to confine its effect.  

3. GIMP (Free/Open Source)  
   • Layer Modes & Opacity  
     – Modes: Overlay, Soft light, Grain merge. Fine-tune opacity to around 30–50%.  
   • Colors→Components→Decompose/Compose  
     – Separate into LAB or HSV planes to selectively adjust only the “A” or “B” channels of your watermark.  
   • Filters→Map→Displace  
     – Use a luminance-based map from your image to subtly warp the watermark.  
   • Filters→Distorts→iWarp  
     – Push/Pull to wrap the logo around curves or panoramic distortions.  
   • Layer Masks & Brushes  
     – Same as Photoshop: soft masks to blend edges or reveal bit-mapped interactions with the scene.  

4. Adobe Illustrator / Inkscape (Vector-centric)  
   • Envelope Distort / Path → Object → Envelope Deform  
     – Wrap a logo over any arbitrary shape or “mesh.”  
   • Warp Effects  
     – Apply effects like Arc, Flag, Bulge to turn a flat watermark into a flowing ribbon element.  
   • Gradient Mesh (AI) / Mesh Gradient (Inkscape)  
     – Create subtle shading and highlights so the logo reads as a physical form in 3D.  
   • Scatter & Art Brushes  
     – Turn your watermark artwork into a scatter brush—sprinkle fragments of it along a path (e.g. a wave or horizon line).  

5. Blender (3D-mapped watermarks)  
   • UV-Map a Plane or Object  
     – Create a simple plane, UV-unwrap, assign your image+watermark texture.  
   • Displacement & Bump  
     – Use the base photo (as a height map) to drive displacement, so the watermark “sits” in the relief.  
   • Light & Shadow Integration  
     – Match HDRI lighting to your photo; the watermark will cast and receive shadows naturally.  
   •  Compositor  
     – After your render, blend over the original photograph with your preferred blend mode.  

6. Coding & Scripting Approaches  
   • Python + OpenCV / PIL  
     – Read both images, resize to match, and do per-pixel alpha blends.  
     – cv2.getPerspectiveTransform + warpPerspective for corner-pinning onto planar surfaces.  
     – Add Gaussian noise or use cv2.addWeighted to simulate film-grain blend.  
   • p5.js / Processing  
     – loadImage() + blend() with MULTIPLY or SCREEN  
     – mask() calls to reveal only parts of the watermark along brightness thresholds  
     – shader( ) to create custom ripple, glitch or feedback patterns.  

7. Quick-Win Plug-Ins & Filters  
   • Nik Collection (Analog Efex, Color Efex): can be clipped to watermark layers for instant stylized grain, tone and color integration.  
   • Topaz Texture Effects: stack textured overlays on your watermark to match canvas or paper media.  
   • ON1 Effects: masking brushes let you restrict effects only to your watermark layer.  

Best Practices  
   • Always match your document’s color profile (sRGB / AdobeRGB) so your watermark’s hues don’t shift.  
   • Save your watermark as a high-resolution asset (vector or 4× your output) to avoid pixelation when warping.  
   • Use non-destructive layers/objects wherever possible—this lets you A/B test or tweak the watermark in situ.  
   • Study your image’s light source, perspective vanishing points and texture resolution, then mimic them when you blend, warp or emboss your mark.  

By choosing the right combination of blend modes, masks, displacement effects, texture/noise and color grading—within the toolchain you’re most comfortable with—you can transform a bolted-on logo into an organic, integral design element.
